source: Fly the same rocket again and again: the mean says what to expect, and the range and standard deviation say how much to trust it.
Students treat one launch as the answer, or confuse the range with the standard deviation.

From the story. The Rocket Boys numbered their rockets, and by May 1960 they had reached Auk XXXI. With many flights to compare, telling a real improvement from luck takes statistics. (More in October Sky.)

Fly the same rocket five times and you get five heights, because wind, launch angle and the motor vary a little. The mean is the typical value. The range (highest minus lowest) is a quick measure of spread. The standard deviation is a better one: roughly the typical distance of a flight from the mean.

$\bar x = \dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}$,   median = middle value in order,   range = max − min,   $s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{n - 1}}$. A change in design is believable when the new mean differs from the old by more than the spread.
Each dot is one launch. The red line is the mean; the gold band is one standard deviation either side.
Heights: $310, 330, 300, 340, 320$ m. Find the mean and standard deviation.
Dividing by $n$ instead of $n - 1$ for a sample, or reporting the range as if it were the standard deviation. The range depends only on the two most extreme flights.
